feed.title: Programming Languages — Useful Sites
feed.subtitle: A hand-curated, annotated link directory across ten areas, from software and AI to security, economics and architecture. Every entry states what the resource does and where it parts ways with its neighbours.

entry.title: Awesome asyncio
entry.summary: A list of libraries and resources for asynchronous I/O in Python 3 (asyncio). Unlike general Python lists, it gathers only event-loop-friendly libraries — web frameworks, database drivers, test tools.

entry.title: Awesome Common Lisp
entry.summary: A list gathering Common Lisp libraries and tools. Unlike browsing the Quicklisp repository one by one, it groups them by domain — web, databases, GUI.

entry.title: Awesome Composer
entry.summary: A list of plugins, tools and guides for Composer, the PHP package manager. Unlike Packagist, it collects not packages but tools that extend Composer itself and improve the workflow.

entry.title: Awesome Coq
entry.summary: A list of libraries, tools and tutorials for Coq (now renamed Rocq), the formal-proof language and environment. Unlike general proof-assistant lists, it covers only the Coq ecosystem.

entry.title: Awesome Elixir
entry.summary: A library list for the Elixir language and Erlang ecosystem. Unlike a Hex package search it is curated and grouped by topic.

entry.title: Awesome Python Scientific Audio
entry.summary: A list of Python libraries for scientific research in audio/music. Unlike general audio tools it is research-oriented: feature extraction, music information retrieval, source separation.

entry.title: Awesome Python Typing
entry.summary: A list of tools and resources for optional static typing in Python. Unlike the mypy docs, it brings together type checkers (mypy, Pyright, Pyre), stub packages and runtime validators.

entry.title: Awesome Ruby
entry.summary: A list gathering Ruby libraries and tools category by category. Unlike a RubyGems search it is curated, current and grouped.

entry.title: Awesome V
entry.summary: A list of libraries, tools and projects for the V language. Unlike Go or Rust lists, it gathers the ecosystem of a still-young language in one place; since the language changes quickly, check how current entries are.

entry.title: C#
entry.summary: Microsoft’s general-purpose language for the .NET platform, and the scripting language of Unity games. Unlike Java, features such as LINQ, async/await and custom value types are built into the language.

entry.title: Dart
entry.summary: Google’s client-oriented language, the one beneath Flutter. Unlike JavaScript it has a sound type system with null safety, and compiles both to native machine code and to JavaScript.

entry.title: Elixir
entry.summary: A functional language on the Erlang VM, strong in scalability. Unlike Erlang it has a Ruby-like syntax and a macro system, while inheriting fault tolerance (OTP) unchanged.

entry.title: Go
entry.summary: The official site of Google’s simple, fast-compiling language, strong in concurrency. Unlike Java or C++ it is deliberately small: few keywords, one formatter (gofmt), builds in seconds.

entry.title: Haskell
entry.summary: A purely functional, statically typed programming language with lazy evaluation. Unlike most functional languages it is pure: side effects are kept apart in the type system (IO).

entry.title: Julia
entry.summary: A high-performance open-source language for scientific computing. Unlike Python it JIT-compiles to near-C speed, aiming to remove the “two-language problem” of prototyping in Python and rewriting hot code in C.

entry.title: Julia.jl
entry.summary: A comprehensive list organising Julia packages and resources by topic. Unlike a package search, it hand-classifies packages by scientific field; some sections may be dated.

entry.title: Lua
entry.summary: A lightweight, embeddable scripting language, common in game engines, embedded systems and Neovim. Unlike Python its runtime is tiny and it embeds easily into a C program.

entry.title: Perl
entry.summary: A dynamic, mature language strong in text processing and system scripting. Unlike Python it has regular expressions built into the language and a one-liner culture; the CPAN archive is vast.

entry.title: PHP
entry.summary: The official docs of one of the web’s most common server-side languages. Unlike most language docs, every function page carries user notes at the bottom — where the practical pitfalls are usually written up.

entry.title: R
entry.summary: A language and environment designed for statistics and data analysis, with tens of thousands of packages on CRAN. Unlike Python, new statistical methods usually appear here first, and it has graphics tools such as ggplot2.

entry.title: Ruby
entry.summary: A multi-paradigm language foregrounding readability and developer happiness — the language of Rails. Unlike Python, everything is an object and its flexible syntax lends itself to DSLs.

entry.title: Swift
entry.summary: Apple’s safe, fast-compiled language, developed primarily for iOS and also running on Linux and servers. Unlike Objective-C it has a safe memory model built around optionals and a modern syntax.

entry.title: CIS 194 Haskell
entry.summary: The University of Pennsylvania’s Haskell course, with lecture notes and assignments public. The difference from a book is the homework — and since Haskell is learned by writing rather than reading, that difference matters.

entry.title: Learn You a Haskell
entry.summary: The community-maintained online edition of the best-known Haskell introduction. Against the academic Haskell texts the difference is tone: it gets to monads through drawings and incremental examples rather than category theory.

entry.title: LearnByExample
entry.summary: Teaches Python, SQL and R through runnable examples, opening each concept with one small piece of code. Against documentation the order is reversed — working example first, explanation after — which also makes it a fast syntax refresher.

entry.title: RubyGems Guides
entry.summary: The official guide to how RubyGems works and how to publish your own gem. Against the API reference it also explains the decisions — version numbering, dependency resolution, publishing policy.

entry.title: JS Exercises
entry.summary: Runnable JavaScript exercises in the browser. Unlike tutorial sites it offers only exercises, no exposition — for consolidating what you have read.

entry.title: Eloquent JavaScript
entry.summary: A free online classic that builds programming thinking rather than teaching syntax, with exercises runnable inside the book itself.

entry.title: A Byte of Python
entry.summary: An introductory Python book, translated into dozens of languages and written for people entirely new to programming. Unlike thick introductory books it is short and direct — done in a few days.

entry.title: Awesome Compilers
entry.summary: A collection of compiler, interpreter and runtime resources, with books, courses and open-source compilers listed separately. Unlike a single textbook, it sets theory, real compiler source and runtime design side by side.

entry.title: Crafting Interpreters
entry.summary: A free book that has you write a language twice — a tree-walking interpreter in Java, then a bytecode VM in C. Unlike theoretical compiler textbooks it makes you write every line; one of the clearest treatments in the field.

entry.title: Hitchhiker’s Guide to Python
entry.summary: A community guide to Python style, project layout and tooling. Unlike the language reference it covers the “how it is written” part: idiomatic code, packaging, testing.

entry.title: kudvenkat
entry.summary: Long, orderly lecture series on .NET, C# and SQL Server. Against short tutorials each series advances like a syllabus — for learning the enterprise .NET stack from nothing.

entry.title: Learn Python
entry.summary: An interactive introduction teaching Python through in-browser exercises, with nothing to install. Against a book, each section ends in an exercise that runs — you see immediately whether it stuck.

entry.title: Learn Shell
entry.summary: An introduction to shell scripting through exercises that run in the browser. Against the shell manuals the difference is that experimenting is free — you can try `rm` without hesitating over what it might hit.

entry.title: Let’s Build A Simple Interpreter
entry.summary: A long series building an interpreter step by step in Python, constructing every piece by hand from lexing to the abstract syntax tree. Unlike Crafting Interpreters, it works in Python on a subset of Pascal.

entry.title: PEP 8
entry.summary: Python’s official style guide, the rules used for the standard library itself. Unlike community guides it is the binding source — the text tools like black and ruff are built on.

entry.title: phpize.online
entry.summary: A playground that runs PHP across versions with MySQL, PostgreSQL or SQLite attached. Unlike other PHP playgrounds it gives you a database, so trying query behaviour needs no server of your own.

entry.title: SICP
entry.summary: Structure and Interpretation of Computer Programs, MIT’s classic text in a readable HTML edition. Unlike books that teach a language it teaches how to build abstractions; Scheme is just the vehicle.

entry.title: The Bash Guide
entry.summary: A guide teaching Bash end to end with the right habits, tackling quoting and word splitting early. That is the break from copy-paste tutorials: most script bugs come from exactly those traps.
